newsitem.title: USA: Mutual fund purchases soar as market steadies.
newsitem.headline: Mutual fund purchases soar as market steadies.

text.p: Mutual fund investors put their feet back on the accelerator pedal in August, as cash inflows jumped sharply.

Analysts said the inflows were helped as jittery investors were calmed by a steadier U.S. stock market between July and August. But they warned that the heady days of huge inflows in the first half of this year are not likely to return.
Investors chose small company growth, growth and income and international funds, after a July infatuation with income and balanced funds, according to Lipper Analytical Services.

The Investment Company Institute, a fund trade group, said Wednesday that preliminary inflows soared to $19.5 billion in August from $4.8 billion in July. Most of the August total, or $19 billion, went into stock funds, versus $5.8 billion in July.

The August sum approached inflows during the first half of this year -- $28.93 billion in January, $22.45 billion in February, $21.41 billion in March, $26.01 billion in April, $25.11 billion in May, and $14.48 billion in June.

The Dow Jones industrial average fell 10 percent during June and July from the mid-May record high, which led buyers to put the brakes on new investments in July, according to analysts. The Dow steadied in August, which served as a balm.
"I don't think the flows are sustainable," said Charles Biderman, president of Trim Tabs Financial Services. "I think you had a mania in the first half."
During that period, investors felt compelled to jump on the bandwagon of a rising market, he said.
Biderman said if first-half flows were sustained for the year, they would total $280 billion, which would account for all new savings generated, and such a trend was not likely.

Some analysts estimated U.S. worker retirement accounts have been sending about $1 billion per month into funds, or about $50 billion annually. They do not expect those flows to drop, but stay steady or rise slightly.
Other monthly inflows can be traced to non-retirement money directly invested by workers.
Analysts also warned that another market correction could send the inflows reeling.

"After the presidential elections, we are expecting some kind of correction around the end of the year," said Brian Blomquist, former chairman of the 100 Percent No-Load Mutual Fund Council and an executive with Ryback Management. "When the market starts to turn, the inflows stop."
But for now, the view is that stocks are again on their way up.

"I think people are still of the belief that the market is going to move higher," said Dan Weiner, president of the Fund Family Shareholders Association, which tracks funds and publishes a newsletter about Vanguard Group funds.

"We've seen people pulling money out of gold funds, and into index funds," Weiner said. "And there's been quite a lot of flow out of income funds, and a little more money flowing into longer-term high income funds."
